title: Safe Equipment Maintenance and Lockout/Tagout
summary: Poorly maintained equipment causes injuries, deaths, and downtime. This talk covers inspecting before use, taking damaged equipment out of service, and controlling hazardous energy.
talking_points: Inspect equipment before every use to confirm it is in safe working order and good repair.
Do not use damaged equipment. Tag it out and take it out of service.
Tell your supervisor when equipment needs maintenance, cleaning, or repair.
Use lockout/tagout to control every hazardous energy source before you maintain, clean, or repair equipment.
Clean up leaks and spills - oil on a step or floor is a slip hazard.
site_hazards_to_check: Hydraulic, fuel, or oil leaks on or under the machine
Damaged equipment still in service with no out-of-service tag
Maintenance or cleaning started without locking out energy sources
Missing or incomplete pre-use inspection records
Slippery steps, grab bars, or work platforms from leaked fluid
discussion_questions: What energy sources need to be locked out on this machine before service?
What do you do when you find a defect during the pre-use inspection?
Who do you report maintenance needs to, and how fast?

attribution.publisher: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
attribution.notice: Adapted from a NIOSH Toolbox Talk (co-developed with CPWR). Public-domain source; not an endorsement by NIOSH or CPWR.

flags: Core mapping is adequate: 29 CFR 1926.600 covers equipment maintenance, incl. 600(a)(3)(ii) (fully lower or block blades, buckets, and dump bodies before repair) and 600(a)(3)(i) (block suspended equipment); 1926.417 covers circuit lockout/tagging. Construction has no general hazardous-energy-control standard equivalent to 1910.147, so the talk's principle - control every energy source (hydraulic, pneumatic, gravity, electrical) before service - is correct practice.

Non-blocking: 29 CFR 1926.431 ('Maintenance of equipment') is narrow (wiring/utilization equipment in hazardous locations) and is a weak fit for a general mechanical/hydraulic maintenance talk; consider replacing it with an explicit 1926.600(a)(3) citation.
